core: What income is — money a person receives, usually from work or investments (working definition, attributed)
Types of income: wages and salaries, self-employment earnings, interest and dividends, government benefits (each one line plus an original example)
Gross income vs net income — before vs after taxes and deductions
Take-home pay — the amount that actually lands in the account
Irregular income — variable hours, freelance, gig work (honest note; budgeting is the sibling topic)
Income and taxes — most income is taxed in some form (one factual line; taxes is the sibling topic)
The honest framing — income is the fuel; the budget decides what it powers

Form W-2 and Form 1099-NEC as reporting forms

claims.claim: Income is the money a person receives, usually from work or investments; the Census Bureau measures money income as income received on a regular basis, before payments for personal income taxes, from sources that include earnings, interest, and dividends.
The main types of income are wages and salaries (pay from an employer), self-employment earnings, interest and dividends (investment income), and government benefits.
Employers pay wages and salaries and provide a Form W-2, Wage and Tax Statement, showing the employee's total wages and withholding.
Self-employment income — earnings from freelance and gig work rather than an employer — is generally reported on Form 1099-NEC rather than a W-2.
Gross income is the whole amount earned before deductions; net income is what remains after deductions are made.
The amount a person earns from a job is different from the amount that arrives in the paycheck.

Take-home pay (net income) is what a worker receives after taxes and deductions are subtracted; typical deductions include income taxes, Social Security and Medicare taxes, retirement-savings contributions, and health-insurance payments.
Earnings can be irregular: hourly pay changes with the hours worked, and self-employment and freelance earnings vary from job to job and month to month.
In the United States, wages, salaries, and tips must be included in gross income, so most income is taxed in some form.

positions: The Census Bureau's money-income measure excludes noncash benefits such as food stamps and subsidized housing
Broader definitions of income include the value of noncash benefits
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the money-income concept: income received as money on a regular basis, before taxes. Government benefits are named among the types, and noncash benefits are out of scope.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The word 'gross' means different things in different contexts
positions: In tax law, gross income means all income from any source
In paycheck contexts, gross pay means earnings before taxes and deductions
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the paycheck context — gross income as earnings before taxes and deductions — which is how the CFPB activity frames gross vs net. Tax-law usage is left to the taxes topic.

sourceRecords.title: Calculating the numbers in your paycheck
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. CFPB youth-financial-education activity (grades 9-12, topic Earn: getting paid, making money, paying taxes). Supports: 'The amount of money you earn from your job is different from the amount of money you receive in your paycheck'; students review a pay stub, calculate tax withholdings and deductions, and compute the difference between gross income and net income. Used to frame the gross-vs-net distinction and take-home pay. Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Earn — MyMoney.gov (U.S. Treasury)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Federal money-management site. Supports: the Earn principle is about more than the amount paid through work — knowing the details of the paycheck, including deductions and withholdings; 'Your take-home pay (net income) is what you receive after any taxes and deductions are subtracted'; typical deductions include federal, state and city income taxes, Social Security and Medicare taxes, retirement-savings contributions, and health insurance payments. Used for the take-home-pay definition and the typical deduction list. Facts restated in original prose.
